items.claim: The seam at Jer.19.14 is a genuine tier-1 boundary, not an under-split of the flask act's own command-performance-interpretation sequence.
items.evidence: Jer.19.11-13 already completes the flask act's own interpretation, extending the doom to Jerusalem's houses and the kings of Judah, so nothing of the sign-act's own exposition remains open when Jer.19.14 opens on a fresh narrative scene-transition (“Then Jeremiah came from Topheth” ... “he stood in the court of Yahweh's house” (web:Jer.19.14)), moving the venue from the Hinnom valley to the temple court and the audience from the escorted elders and priests to “all the people” in the same verse (web:Jer.19.14) - an explicit scene and addressee shift, not a continuation of the act's own three-phase structure. The closing verdict at Jer.19.15 restates the coming judgment in general terms rather than elaborating the jar symbolism, consistent with a fresh narrative report closing the complex rather than the sign-act's own interpretive coda. Both Hebrew quotes collate at byte tier against the source text; the setumah at Jer.19.14 and the petuchah at the preceding Jer.19.13 check correctly against the mark inventory as tier-3, single-witness corroboration, never a boundary driver.

items.claim: Jer.20.1-6 is correctly kept as one incident, and the two Pashhurs relevant to this span are correctly kept distinct by patronymic.
items.evidence: The striking-and-stocks scene (Jer.20.1-2) and the next-day release-and-renaming scene (Jer.20.3-6) share one participant pair and report one incident; no discourse-frame imperative, addressee shift, or date header marks the day-change, so the granularity rule gives no warrant to cut there. Jer.20.1 names “Pashhur, the son of Immer the priest” explicitly (web:Jer.20.1), distinguishing him by patronymic from “Pashhur the son of Malchijah” introduced in the following frame (web:Jer.21.1); nothing in this span conflates the two or transfers one man's narrative onto the other. Both Hebrew quotes collate at byte tier; the petuchah at Jer.20.3 and setumah at Jer.20.6 check correctly against the mark inventory.

items.claim: Keeping Jer.20.7-18 whole, with the praise-to-curse pivot at Jer.20.13/14 held open rather than resolved, is the correct treatment of a genuinely unmarked internal edge.
items.evidence: No koh-amar restart, addressee shift, scene change, date header, or vision opening marks the turn from the doxology (“Sing to Yahweh! Praise Yahweh”, web:Jer.20.13) to the self-curse (“Cursed is the day in which I was born”, web:Jer.20.14); an abrupt tonal reversal alone does not license a cut under the granularity rule, so keeping the whole confession as one unit rather than atomizing it at an unmarked pivot is correct. The span also lines up as the fifth of five individually named confession spans (sweep: 5 spans) in the governing frame architecture (Jer.11.18-12.6, 15.10-21, 17.14-18, 18.18-23, 20.7-18), confirming the unit's own boundaries independently of the internal-pivot question. Medium confidence with the frontier flag set is the honest calibration for a held-open internal edge rather than a false resolution. Both Hebrew quotes collate at byte tier; the setumah marks at Jer.20.6, Jer.20.12, and Jer.20.13, and the petuchah closing at Jer.20.18, check out correctly, verse by verse, against the mark inventory.

items.claim: The frame seam is correctly placed at Jer.21.1 on the book's own frame-opening word-event marker, and the embedded koh-amar reply at Jer.21.4 is correctly kept inside the narrative embassy report rather than split out.
items.evidence: Jer.21.1 opens on “The word which came to Jeremiah from Yahweh” (web:Jer.21.1), a member of the book's eleven-verse prose-sermon-superscription word-event class - the frame-opening spine itself - giving this boundary top-tier warrant; the row does not straddle it. Jeremiah's answer at Jer.21.4 carries its own koh-amar onset but no frame-owner change, since Yahweh continues speaking through Jeremiah to the same royal delegation named at the opening; a bare koh-amar restart without a change of whose mouth carries it does not by itself license a cut, so keeping the embassy's question and Jeremiah's answer in one narrative unit is correct rather than an under-split. “Pashhur the son of Malchijah” (web:Jer.21.1) is again named by patronymic, keeping this royal envoy distinct from the priest struck in the previous frame. Both Hebrew quotes collate at byte tier; the petuchah at Jer.20.18 and setumah at Jer.21.2 check correctly against the mark inventory.

items.claim: The re-commission at Jer.21.8 is an explicit, well-marked addressee shift and correctly opens its own row separate from the royal reply just closed.
items.evidence: Jer.21.1-7 addresses Zedekiah's own delegation; Jer.21.8 opens with an instruction to Jeremiah naming a new target audience, “You shall say to this people” (web:Jer.21.8), before the koh-amar oracle itself begins - an overt re-addressing clause, not merely a continuation of the same reported exchange, so the cut is warranted under the explicit-addressee-shift category on its own, independent of any koh-amar-with-frame-owner-change reading. The oracle's own closing line, “I have set my face on this city for evil, and not for good” (web:Jer.21.10), keeps the judgment_oracle classification apt. Both Hebrew quotes collate at byte tier; the setumah closing the row at Jer.21.10 checks correctly against the mark inventory, and no mark falls on the verse just before the row opens.

items.claim: Keeping Jer.21.11-14 as one royal-house oracle is correct; the pointed text does shift address across the span, but the shift follows a recognized prophetic pattern rather than marking a scene change, and the rejected alternative discloses the narrowing rather than concealing it.
items.evidence: The address does move across this span: Jer.21.12 uses plural forms addressing “House of David” collectively (דִּ֤ינוּ לַבֹּ֨קֶר֙ מִשְׁפָּ֔ט [oshb:Jer.21.12, byte tier] near “Execute justice in the morning,” web:Jer.21.12), while Jer.21.13 turns to a feminine-singular address to Jerusalem herself (הִנְנִ֨י אֵלַ֜יִךְ יֹשֶׁ֧בֶת הָעֵ֛מֶק [oshb:Jer.21.13, byte tier] near “Behold, I am against you, O inhabitant of the valley,” web:Jer.21.13). That oscillation between addressing a royal house collectively and addressing its city as a personified entity within one sustained oracle is a recognized prophetic pattern, not a scene change on its own, and the rejected alternative correctly concedes that the referent narrows from the dynasty to the city itself rather than denying any shift occurs. No discourse-frame imperative, scene break, or koh-amar with a changed frame-owner falls at the join, so the granularity rule gives no warrant to cut there. Neum-YHWH closes the unit twice (Jer.21.13, Jer.21.14), and a fresh discourse-frame commissioning imperative follows immediately at Jer.22.1 (“Go down to the house of the king of Judah”, web:Jer.22.1); neum-YHWH's closure reading depends on a fresh tier-1 onset following, which is satisfied here. Both Hebrew quotes collate at byte tier; the setumah before the row at Jer.21.10 and the setumah closing it at Jer.21.14 check correctly against the mark inventory.

items.claim: The rejected alternative overclaims that the Jer.22.6 koh-amar restart changes neither frame-owner nor addressee; the pointed text shows a real shift from plural address to a singular personified address that the stated warrant does not engage.
items.evidence: Jer.22.2-5 sustains plural address to the king together with his household (e.g. עֲשׂ֤וּ מִשְׁפָּט֙ [oshb:Jer.22.3, byte tier] near “Execute justice” web:Jer.22.3, and Jer.22.2's own “who sits on David's throne” web:Jer.22.2), but Jer.22.6 opens a fresh koh-amar restart naming “concerning the house of the king of Judah” (web:Jer.22.6) again and immediately addresses a singular “you”: גִּלְעָ֥ד אַתָּ֛ה לִ֖י (oshb:Jer.22.6, byte tier) near “You are Gilead to me” (web:Jer.22.6), continued in the singular at Jer.22.7 (עָלֶ֛יךָ [oshb:Jer.22.7, byte tier] near “against you” web:Jer.22.7). That is a real addressee shift in grammatical number, not the absence of one the rejected alternative states ("it reopens without a change of frame-owner or addressee"). A stronger warrant for keeping the span whole would rest on the same recognized prophetic pattern used elsewhere in this span, of addressing a royal house both as its living occupants (plural) and as a personified singular dwelling within one oracle - the pattern this span's own earlier oracle uses between the dynasty and the personified city (Jer.21.11-14) - rather than on a flat denial that the address changes. The Jer.22.6 restart also repeats the same framing that opened the earlier oracle, “Concerning the house of the king of Judah” (web:Jer.21.11), where that framing accompanied a fresh row; the rationale does not address why the same framing does not do the same work here. High confidence is not well supported once the addressee shift is accounted for; medium would better match the evidence actually cited. This does not by itself show the span should be split - the personification pattern is a genuine textual basis for keeping it whole - but the stated rejected alternative needs correction to the real grounds rather than a denial the bytes do not support.

items.claim: The mourning-instruction imperative at Jer.22.10 is a well-marked discourse-frame onset, correctly separated from the palace oracle before it and resolved to a named individual within the row.
items.evidence: Jer.22.9 closes the preceding oracle on the nations' own question-and-answer formula, third-person and without a direct addressee; Jer.22.10 opens on a fresh negative discourse imperative (“Don't weep for the dead”, web:Jer.22.10) that is immediately resolved at Jer.22.11 to a specific named figure, “Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned instead of Josiah his father,” (web:Jer.22.11) distinguished by patronymic and regnal note from the other named kings nearby. The row closes cleanly before the next oracle's own hoy woe-onset at Jer.22.13, so both boundaries are well warranted. Both Hebrew quotes collate at byte tier; the setumah closing the verse before the row (Jer.22.9) and the setumah marks at the row's own opening (Jer.22.10) and close (Jer.22.12) check correctly against the mark inventory.
